cards.title: Diagnose Growth Bottlenecks Through a Data-Integrity First Lens
cards.summary: Treat business growth as a sequence of bottlenecks and use trustworthy data to find the current one before spending more on creative or account structure.
cards.use_when: You feel like the store is 'on a treadmill' — dashboards show improving ROAS but profit and revenue are flat, and you need to decide where to focus resources (merchandise, creative, media, retention) next quarter.
steps: Frame the business as three stacked pillars: data integrity/measurement at the base, creative velocity/diversity in the middle, technical account structure on top. The source argues the upper layers are meaningless if the base is wrong, because you'll be optimizing creative and budgets against false signals.

Recognize that a business grows by repeatedly solving one bottleneck at a time — when one is solved, another appears. So the recurring task is not 'do everything' but 'find the current constraint fast' and resource it.

Use accurate, commercially-aligned data to locate the bottleneck: platform-reported ROAS, CPA and multi-touch numbers are the least reliable tier; finance-grade metrics (profit contribution, MER/AMER) are more reliable; controlled lift studies are the most causal but slowest to read.

Example of the failure mode: an ad reads 4x ROAS, so you brief more ads like it and increase spend; ROAS dips to 3x but you reinforce the same decision. If the original 4x was inflated, every downstream decision (creative briefs, budget shifts, staffing) is wrong while profit stays flat.

Practical output: before allocating next quarter's resource, verify which pillar is actually failing — if you cannot reconcile marketing claims to the P&L, data integrity is the bottleneck regardless of what the channel dashboards say.
caveats: The claim that data integrity is the bottleneck in ~30% of audited businesses is the presenter's own audit experience, not a universal benchmark.
The 2026 framing (iOS deprecation, modeled conversions) is time-specific; verify current platform behavior before relying on details.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Stop Northstar-ing on Platform-Reported ROAS
cards.summary: Platform ROAS is not comparable across campaigns, platforms or funnel stages because each read reflects different margins, attribution models and funnel positions.
cards.use_when: You are setting KPI targets, evaluating channel performance, or deciding how to reallocate budget across Meta, Google, Pinterest or TikTok.
steps: Recognize that equal ROAS ≠ equal profit. Two campaigns can each report $10,000 in attributed revenue at the same ROAS, but if one used a discount code and lower-margin products, its profit contribution differs materially from a full-price retention campaign. Compare profit contribution per campaign, not ROAS, before shifting spend.

Never compare ROAS across platforms. Pinterest, for example, counts view-through conversions and can claim a conversion if any ad tile is on screen — the source notes it often serves warm audiences who would have bought anyway, inflating its read versus Meta's. So a 7x Pinterest vs 2.5x Meta is not a valid reason to move budget to Pinterest.

Understand funnel position: a cold top-of-funnel campaign at 2x can be far more valuable than a bottom-of-funnel retargeting campaign at 7x, because growth requires continuously injecting spend at the top. Pulling top-of-funnel spend to fund high-ROAS bottom-funnel will eventually collapse the business.

Watch the cross-platform halo effect: launching TikTok at ~25% of Meta budget at 1-2x can make a Meta mid-funnel campaign jump from 4x to 12x because TikTok traffic is being retargeted on Meta. If you interpret that as 'Meta is performing, let's scale Meta,' you will waste budget — the lift came from TikTok.
The source's position: if you are northstar-ing on platform ROAS, you are roughly three years behind competitors who have moved to commercially-aligned metrics.
caveats: The presenter states this view as a strong opinion from 1,000+ audits; the exact attribution behavior of each platform changes and should be verified.
The '3 years behind' framing is a rhetorical claim, not a measured benchmark.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Cut the Three Sources of ROAS Over-Inflation
cards.summary: View-through attribution, existing-customer bleed-over and third-party halo effects all inflate platform ROAS above true incremental impact.
cards.use_when: You suspect your reported ROAS is too good to be true, or you are auditing why higher ad spend is not translating to higher profit.
steps: 1) View-through conversions. Meta defaults to 7-day click / 1-day view (and 1-day engaged). The 1-day view counts a conversion if someone merely saw the ad and bought within 24 hours — no click or interaction required. This is where much over-attribution comes from, especially for people already familiar with the brand who would have bought anyway.

2) Existing-customer bleed-over. If existing customers are served in 'cold' campaigns, their purchases get credited to those campaigns even though they would likely have repeated anyway (e.g., a supplement customer buying when their pack runs out). Check that customer lists are actually excluded from acquisition campaigns.

3) Third-party halo effects. Off-platform activations (pop-up, retail, an event in New York) can triple digital performance in that region. Without knowing the activation happened, the ad account looks causal when it is merely correlated. Do not pump spend into a region purely because ROAS spiked if an external event overlaps.

Inflation compounds with business maturity: more existing customers, more channels (including retail stores that function like advertising) and larger organic presence all inflate paid reads. The bigger the business, the less reliable platform ROAS becomes at any funnel level.
caveats: Source is the presenter's audit experience; magnitude of each effect varies by brand. Retail/organic halo effects are especially relevant for omnichannel businesses, less so for pure direct-to-consumer startups.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Set Meta Attribution Windows to 7-Day Click / 1-Day Engaged
cards.summary: Removing 1-day view-through from Meta reporting produces a ROAS read that correlates more tightly with P&L efficiency.
cards.use_when: You are configuring Meta campaign reporting or diagnosing why Meta ROAS does not reconcile with actual profit.
steps: Check the current default: Meta typically reports on 7-day click, 1-day view, 1-day engaged. The view-through component is the main source of over-attribution.

Recommendation from source: move campaigns to 7-day click / 1-day engaged and drop 1-day view. You can also do this reporting-only by going to Columns → Compare Attribution Settings → select 7-day click reporting, without changing campaign delivery.

Reason to keep 1-day engaged: Meta redefined '7-day click' around March-April 2026 so it now requires an outbound click to the website. Previously, likes, comments, shares or page clicks counted as clicks. Those engagement interactions moved into '1-day engaged.' Including 1-day engaged preserves a click-like signal that likely has a causal relationship.

Expect an immediate drop in reported ROAS when you remove view-throughs — the source says 7-day click ROAS numbers got worse overnight after the definition change. This is a correction, not a performance decline. Verify the current Meta interface and definitions before making changes, as these settings change over time.
caveats: Platform interfaces and attribution definitions change frequently — verify current settings before applying. The source's own dates (early 2026) may already be outdated.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Use Meta Incremental Attribution as Directional, Not Definitive
cards.summary: Meta's incremental attribution is an industry-benchmark estimate built from competitors' lift tests, not a live holdout measurement in your account.
cards.use_when: You want a more causal channel read but cannot afford a full geo-lift or platform lift test, and are deciding whether to trust the incremental attribution column.
steps: Read it in Meta via Columns → Compare Attribution Settings → Incremental Attribution, broken out by campaign.

How it works conceptually: Meta models a holdout — if 2% of exposed users purchase and 1% of non-exposed users still purchase, the difference (2% − 1% = 1%) is the incremental rate. A reported 5x ROAS would become 2.5x incremental ROAS in that example.

Critical caveat: Meta does not run these holdouts in real time in your account. It applies a factor derived from conversion lift experiments run by competitors in your niche/industry. So it is not an accurate real-lift outcome for your account — treat it as directional guidance on which campaigns are genuinely additive.

For smaller brands where almost nobody knows you, the non-exposed purchase rate will be near zero; for mature brands with big repeat bases, a meaningful share of 'non-exposed' users will still buy, which is exactly what makes the incremental read lower than the platform read.
caveats: The presenter emphasizes the mechanism is applied from competitor benchmarks, so results are estimates. Verify current Meta documentation since this feature is relatively new.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Build a Metric Hierarchy Instead of Adding More Dashboards
cards.summary: Subtract metrics rather than add them — the goal is the fewest commercially-aligned KPIs that allow clear decisions.
cards.use_when: Your team has multiple attribution tools and dashboards producing conflicting reads, and meetings stall because no one agrees which number is right.
steps: Diagnose the symptom: if one person says Triple Whale shows Pinterest is bad, another says an incrementality test says it's good, and a third says causal inference says something else, you have too many confounded metrics rather than too little data.

Apply the pyramid of reliability: (bottom) attributed platform numbers like ROAS and CPA — fast but unreliable; (middle) finance-grade metrics — profit contribution, MER, AMER; (top) lift studies with control and treatment groups — most causal but slowest to read.

Match decision size to metric tier. Use platform metrics for quick day-to-day directional decisions only when you understand their attribution nuances. Use lift studies or finance-grade metrics for large budget, channel or strategy decisions.

Practical output: a single dashboard with profit contribution (or new-customer profit contribution) as the headline, AMER and new-customer revenue/orders beside it, plus CAC and profit contribution below. This gives high accuracy because it is based on actual financials, and it prevents the 'adding more data' trap the source says most teams fall into.
The source's position: adding third-party attribution tools generally compounds confusion rather than solving it, because perfect cross-platform user-journey tracking is unknowable.
caveats: Source is a strong practitioner opinion. Some teams with very large spend may still find third-party tooling useful for specific questions, but the source argues against it.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Distinguish MER from AMER to Avoid False Scaling Decisions
cards.summary: Total MER can rise on returning-customer revenue while new-customer acquisition quietly deteriorates; AMER isolates the acquisition spend's true efficiency.
cards.use_when: You review monthly marketing efficiency and are deciding whether to increase (or cut) media budget.
steps: Define MER as net revenue / ad spend (or the inverse as a percentage of revenue allocated to marketing). Always use net revenue — subtract returns — especially in fashion where returns process later and would otherwise compress tomorrow's read.
Define AMER as new-customer net revenue / ad spend. New-customer revenue is the part paid media is actually responsible for, because advertising drives acquisition, not returning-customer repeat.

Worked example from source: In January MER = 4x; in February it rises to 5x, so you increase March spend. But AMER was 2.0x, then 1.8x, then 1.6x — the February MER rise came from a returning-customer bump while new-customer revenue was falling. Scaling on the MER signal erodes new-customer acquisition and profits further. This pattern is common in audits.

Use MER as a CFO allocation-control metric (percentage of P&L to marketing, alongside gross margin and opex, to hit a profit target). Do not hold the CMO accountable to total MER because most ad spend drives new, not returning, revenue.

Remember the source's warning that acquisition MER targets are not universal: a 60%-gross-margin business with strong retention can sustain a lower AMER than a 40%-margin business with weak retention. Judge AMER against margin profile and repeat rates, not a fixed number.
caveats: AMER becomes less reliable as more channels and offline spend (influencers, retail) are added; source says that is when lift studies are needed. 'AMER is not equal' across businesses is the presenter's core caveat.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Track New-Customer Revenue, Orders, CAC and Profit Contribution
cards.summary: A compact set of finance-grade metrics shows whether acquisition is growing, efficient and profitable — the core of an executive dashboard.
cards.use_when: You are designing your weekly or monthly store performance dashboard and want metrics that tie directly to profit rather than platform attribution.
steps: Track new-customer revenue separately from total revenue to see volume growth. Most brands do not do this independently.
Track new-customer orders alongside revenue, because revenue can diverge from orders when average order value shifts.

Track CAC = total ad spend / new customers acquired. Note that acquisition MER is generally the better profitability measure because it encapsulates average order value, while CAC does not. CAC is useful as a leading indicator: when it moves, investigate what changed in the product portfolio or mix.

Track profit contribution = revenue − cost of delivery − marketing expense (in dollars, or in percentages minus the percentage equivalents). Then going further, compute new-customer profit contribution = new-customer revenue − its delivery cost − its marketing cost, which tells you whether acquisition is profitable.

Arrange the dashboard: profit contribution (or new-customer profit contribution) as the headline metric; AMER and new-customer revenue/orders beside it; CAC and profit contribution figures below. The source argues this is enough to know whether the last week's decisions were good and whether to course correct.
caveats: Source warns these finance-grade metrics lose reliability for high-eight- to nine-figure businesses with many channels (e.g., $1M/month on influencers you can't attribute), where lift studies become necessary. Requires accurate cost-of-delivery data to be valid.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Use LTGP:CAC as a Comparable Cross-Business Metric
cards.summary: A ratio linking lifetime gross profit to acquisition cost is comparable across time and across businesses, unlike MER or AMER.
cards.use_when: You want to self-benchmark historically, compare portfolio or competitor efficiency, or decide how aggressively to scale acquisition.
steps: Compute long-term gross profit (LTGP) over a chosen window divided by CAC. Ratios are superior because each side contextualizes the other — CAC alone or LTGP alone has no context.

Choose the window: if comparing only against yourself, 30-, 90- or 180-day windows are fine. If comparing across businesses or industries, extend the window because retention profiles differ (a CPG brand may have a low first-purchase GP:CAC but higher repeat, while fashion may differ).

Use the source's 180-day benchmarks as heuristics, not rules: below 1.0x is very bad (equivalent to >6-month CAC payback, which the presenter says he would avoid); 1-2x is okay/acceptable but not efficient (either CAC too high or GP too low); 2-3x is where you want to be and should scale; 3x+ the source frames as 'bad' because you are leaving money on the table — with the qualification that a genuine cash-flow constraint is a valid reason not to scale.

For ecommerce application: if you are at 3x+ on 180-day LTGP:CAC, prioritize budget increases into current acquisition channels rather than adding new channels; fix cash flow before taking large loans to scale.
caveats: The numeric bands are the source's heuristics (presenter's opinion), not a formula-derived benchmark. '3x is bad' is a strong opinion tied to the presenter's view on opportunity cost; some operators will reasonably disagree.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Tag COGS in Shopify to See Real-Time Gross Margin Compression
cards.summary: Without tagged cost of goods you cannot see margin compression during discount events, so profit, LTGP and contribution metrics will be wrong.
cards.use_when: You are preparing for Black Friday or any discount event and relying on a fixed gross-margin assumption in your reporting or agency models.
steps: Tag cost of goods on all products in Shopify so you get real-time gross margin visibility, and can flow it to external software or Google Sheets reporting.

Why it matters with a worked example: a $100 product with $50 cost of delivery has $50 GP (50%). At 20% off, price falls to $80 while cost of delivery stays $50, so GP compresses to $30 and gross margin to 30/80 = 37.5% — a 12.5-point drop, roughly a 30% relative decline. Average order value may rise from bigger baskets, but per-unit margin is what drives gross margin.

If you instead assume 50% margin everywhere (e.g., you told your agency 'average margin is 50%'), all your profitable models are wrong during discount periods, and every downstream metric — profit contribution, LTGP:CAC, AMER — is misstated.

For ecommerce application: before running a storewide sale, re-run your key reports with the discount-adjusted margin to see if the promotion still clears your contribution target; review which products drive most of the margin compression.
caveats: Requires accurate per-SKU cost data, which many brands lack — the source notes this as a common audit finding. Service-cost allocation to individual orders may need judgment.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Run a Geo-Lift Experiment to Measure True Incremental ROAS
cards.summary: A controlled state/region test with a counterfactual prediction reveals the causal revenue impact of a spend change when attribution is confounded.
cards.use_when: You are a larger brand deciding how much budget to put into a channel, or whether a top-of-funnel investment (TikTok, OOH, YouTube) actually drives revenue.
steps: Select regions by clustering. Use historical ad spend, new-customer revenue and new-customer orders — include orders because revenue can diverge from orders via AOV swings. Do not require a single state to match another; combine states into groups that move together historically. Arizona + Texas vs New York + California is the source's illustrative example.

Build a predictive model: the control group's history should predict the treatment group's baseline with very high accuracy (source cites ~99%). This is your counterfactual — what the treatment would have done without intervention.
Apply the intervention to treatment states only (e.g., 2x or 3x budget on a Meta cold campaign, or launch TikTok in treatment states). Keep control states untouched.

After the period, compare actual treatment revenue against the counterfactual prediction. The difference is the incremental lift. If lift is $100,000 and you spent an extra $40,000, incremental ROAS is 2.5x.
You can also measure multiple revenue streams in this framework — e.g., check whether retail revenue in treatment states diverges from control — and re-run with different states for subsequent tests.
caveats: In Australia the source says state-level geo-lift is poor: you need massive spend and cannot re-run soon without muddying the clustering data — use commuting-zone-level regions instead. Geo-lift requires sufficient spend and data volume to be meaningful.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Understand Platform Lift Tests vs External Geo-Lift Tests
cards.summary: In-platform lift tests split at the user level; external geo-lift splits at the region level — each has different trust and cost trade-offs.
cards.use_when: You want to validate a channel's incremental impact but need to choose between running a Meta/TikTok/Google lift test or building your own geo-lift.
steps: In-platform lift tests (Meta, Google, TikTok): these split control and treatment at the individual user ID level, so some users see ads and others don't; the platform then measures whether non-exposed users still purchase. This avoids the need for regional separation.

Cost and access: source says Meta allows these fairly readily and they can be run often. TikTok and Google typically impose minimum spend (source cites roughly $200k for TikTok) before they'll run the test.

Key disadvantage: in-platform lift tests rely entirely on the platform's own data science and measurement — you are trusting Meta, TikTok or Google to give an accurate read. External geo-lift (see counterpart card) measures against your own revenue and avoids that dependency.

For ecommerce application: use in-platform lift tests for ongoing quick validation of Meta (your largest channel, per the source typically 60-70% of spend), and use external geo-lift when you need a defensible cross-channel or top-of-funnel read — especially before committing to TV, OOH or a new channel.
caveats: Minimum spend requirements change over time and vary by platform and region — verify current thresholds. The source notes in-platform results depend on trusting the platform's methodology.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Don't Chase First-Click or Third-Party Attribution Truth
cards.summary: The most valuable journey points are first and last click, but first click is effectively unknowable and third-party tools add confusion rather than truth.
cards.use_when: You are evaluating third-party attribution tools or deciding how to allocate budget between brand search, top-of-funnel and bottom-of-funnel campaigns.
steps: Last click you already have accurately in-platform: you know when people click and buy without a third-party tool.

First click is nearly impossible to track accurately. The source, after hundreds of hours in attribution tools, reports seeing absurd results — e.g., 'first click came from brand search' for a customer whose actual first exposure was a friend wearing the product (viral/word-of-mouth). Cookies and identifiers break somewhere along the chain.

Danger: if you trust the tool that says brand search is the first click, you put more spend into brand search. But the real driver was whatever caused awareness before the brand search — the top-of-funnel activity or word-of-mouth.

Practical allocation: crank top-of-funnel spend on how people initially hear about you, and modulate bottom-of-funnel enough to capture conversion. Do not use first-click attribution to justify shifting budget to brand search or low-funnel channels.
Overall position: adding third-party attribution tools compounds internal confusion; subtract rather than add.
caveats: The presenter states not to rely on third-party attribution tools at all — a strong opinion. Some large brands may still find specific tool outputs useful, but the source argues the first-click read is fundamentally unreliable.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Reconcile Platform Data Against the P&L
cards.summary: The core discipline of data integrity is tying platform metrics back to actual financial outcomes so decisions rest on the P&L, not on attribution reads.
cards.use_when: You are auditing your measurement setup or preparing a board/CFO review of marketing spend efficiency.
steps: Start from the P&L and work backwards: profit contribution = revenue − cost of delivery − marketing. New-customer profit contribution = new-customer revenue − its delivery cost − its marketing cost.
Ask whether the platform-reported numbers can defend themselves internally: which metric would you stand behind if the CFO challenged whether a channel actually drove revenue?
For churn-heavy or high-return categories (fashion, supplements), use net revenue rather than gross revenue — returns will otherwise make today's ROAS look good and tomorrow's P&L worse.

Build a single reconciled view: CFO headline = profit contribution; then AMER, new-customer revenue/orders; then CAC; then profit contribution detail. High accuracy comes from basing metrics on actual financials rather than modeled attribution.

Where platform and P&L disagree, investigate before scaling: often platform ROAS is inflated by view-through, existing-customer bleed-over or a halo event. Don't add another attribution tool to resolve the gap — subtract noise and reconcile to financials.
caveats: Source says finance-grade reconciliation loses reliability as the business introduces more channels and complexity; above roughly high-eight-figure scale, lift studies may be required to attribute revenue to specific channels.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx

cards.title: Audit for the Common Tracking Infrastructure Failures
cards.summary: Recurring measurement mistakes — view-through defaults, untagged COGS, customer-list leakage, missing CAPI — recur across audits and should be checked systematically.
cards.use_when: You are running an internal audit or ad-account health check and want a repeatable list of things to verify.
steps: Check Meta attribution windows: is 1-day view still enabled? Move to 7-day click / 1-day engaged or switch reporting to 7-day click to remove view-through noise.
Verify existing customers are excluded from cold/acquisition campaigns. Look for campaign structures where customer lists are not actually applied, causing bleed-over and inflated read.
Confirm COGS is tagged in Shopify for every product so gross margin and profit contribution are real, not assumptions. This is required for LTGP:CAC, profit contribution and discount-margin analysis.

Ensure CAPI (Conversions API) is set up so first-party event data is sent server-side, bypassing iOS restrictions — the source identifies event matching via CAPI as necessary infrastructure in the post-iOS-14 environment.
Check whether ad-spend halo effects from off-platform activity (retail, pop-ups, events) coincide with ROAS spikes; flag them in reporting so you don't mistake correlation for causation.

Verify attribution windows on each platform (Google often 30-day click plus view/engage windows; Meta/TikTok defaults differ) so you understand the incrementality factor behind any number before comparing.
caveats: Platform defaults and definitions change frequently — verify current settings. This card reflects the presenter's audit observations and may not apply to every account.
cards.source_name: The #1 Bottleneck I See in 80% of eCommerce Audits.docx
